paragraphs.title: Habakkuk’s Cry Over Evil and Injustice

easy.explanation: The first verse identifies Habakkuk as the prophet.
easy.q: Who is identified as the prophet in the opening verse?

easy.explanation: Habakkuk cries out about violence, iniquity, strife, and suffering.
easy.q: What does Habakkuk cry to the LORD about?

easy.explanation: Habakkuk says that wrong judgment proceeds.
easy.q: What happens to judgment according to Habakkuk?

answers: He sees violence but does not see deliverance
He wishes to begin a war
medium.explanation: He cries about violence while saying that the LORD does not save.
medium.q: Why does Habakkuk repeatedly call upon the LORD?

answers: The law is weakened and no longer properly effective
medium.explanation: The phrase describes a time when the law does not function properly in society.
medium.q: What does “the law is slacked” mean in this passage?

answers: The wicked surround the righteous, so judgment is perverted
The righteous surround the wicked, so judgment becomes stronger
medium.explanation: Habakkuk connects the wicked surrounding the righteous with wrong judgment.
medium.q: How are wickedness and distorted judgment connected?

answers: Confusion and lament over God’s silence
challenge.explanation: Habakkuk asks why God sees violence without bringing deliverance.
challenge.q: What central feeling emerges from Habakkuk’s words?

answers: The problem affects only private disputes
Evil damages the whole system of justice
Judgment has no connection with society
challenge.explanation: The passage describes both social violence and corruption of the legal order.
challenge.q: What does the movement from violence and strife to wrong judgment show?

answers: The wicked surround and oppress the righteous
challenge.explanation: The wicked are said to compass about, or surround, the righteous.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between “the wicked” and “the righteous” in this passage?

paragraphs.title: The Rise of the Chaldeans and Their Conquering Power

easy.explanation: The LORD says, “I raise up the Chaldeans.”
easy.q: Which people does the LORD say He will raise up?

easy.explanation: They are called a bitter and hasty nation and are described as terrible and dreadful.
They scoff at strongholds, heap up dust, and take them.
easy.q: What do the Chaldeans do to strongholds?

medium.explanation: Dwellingplaces are homes or inhabited places.
medium.q: What does “dwellingplaces” mean in this passage?

answers: Because the LORD will do an astonishing work they would not believe
Because the nations are preparing a celebration
medium.explanation: The LORD announces a remarkable work that would not be believed if merely reported.
medium.q: Why are the nations told to behold, regard, and wonder?

answers: They do not leave their own country
medium.explanation: Their horses are swifter than leopards, and they fly like an eagle.
medium.q: How do the Chaldeans move through the land?

challenge.explanation: These comparisons highlight the army’s speed, fierceness, and hunger for conquest.
challenge.q: What do the comparisons to leopards, evening wolves, and an eagle emphasize?

challenge.explanation: They scoff at kings and make princes a scorn.
challenge.q: How do the Chaldeans treat kings and princes?

answers: Their military power, which they credit to their god
challenge.explanation: At the end of the passage, they impute their power to their god.
challenge.q: What is the source of the Chaldeans’ confidence according to the passage?

paragraphs.title: Habakkuk Questions the Use of the Wicked

easy.explanation: Habakkuk addresses the LORD as his God and Holy One.
easy.q: To whom does Habakkuk speak and whom does he call holy?

answers: The LORD’s eyes are purer than to behold evil
easy.explanation: Habakkuk says that the LORD is of purer eyes than to behold evil.
easy.q: How does Habakkuk describe the LORD’s attitude toward evil?

answers: As fish and creeping things without a ruler
easy.explanation: He compares people to fish and creeping things that have no ruler over them.
easy.q: How does Habakkuk describe human beings?

answers: How the wicked can devour someone more righteous than themselves
Why the righteous rule over the wicked
Why there are no fish in the sea
medium.explanation: Habakkuk struggles with the wicked devouring people who are more righteous than they are.
medium.q: What central difficulty does Habakkuk bring before the LORD?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to people acting faithlessly and wickedly toward others.
medium.q: What does “deal treacherously” mean in this context?

answers: To say that the LORD cannot hear
medium.explanation: The title stresses that the LORD has existed eternally.
medium.q: Why does Habakkuk call the LORD “from everlasting”?

answers: A pure God allows the wicked to harm the righteous
A weak nation defeats every other nation
The righteous do not know the law
challenge.explanation: Habakkuk struggles with the contrast between God’s purity and the success of the wicked.

answers: They are vulnerable and without a ruler
They are stronger than the conqueror
challenge.explanation: The image emphasizes their helplessness and lack of governing protection.
challenge.q: What does the image of people as fish and creeping things suggest?

answers: He wants to understand God’s silence before injustice
He wants to praise the conqueror
He cannot see what is happening
challenge.explanation: The questions express his perplexity that God sees the evil but does not immediately intervene.
challenge.q: Why does Habakkuk ask, “wherefore lookest thou” and “holdest thy tongue”?

paragraphs.title: The Fisherman Metaphor and the Question of Limits

easy.explanation: The conqueror is described as catching people with an angle, net, and drag.
easy.q: What is the Babylonian conqueror compared to?

easy.explanation: The passage says that he rejoices and is glad.
easy.q: How does the conqueror respond to his catch?

answers: Whether the conqueror will continue killing nations without mercy
Whether the fish will return to the sea
easy.explanation: Habakkuk asks whether the conqueror will continually empty his net and slay the nations.
easy.q: What does Habakkuk ask at the end of the chapter?

answers: The conqueror’s tools of capture and warfare
The worship tools of the righteous
medium.explanation: They represent the means by which the conqueror captures and subdues people.
medium.q: What do the angle, net, and drag represent in the metaphor?

answers: A net used for catching fish
medium.explanation: A drag is a fishing net used to gather fish.
medium.q: What is a “drag” in this passage?

answers: He credits them with his success and abundance
medium.explanation: He treats his instruments of conquest as the source of his prosperity and plentiful food.
medium.q: Why does the conqueror sacrifice to his net and burn incense to his drag?

answers: He turns his power and weapons into idols
He admits that he has no power
He asks the nations for peace
challenge.explanation: He gives credit for his success to his net and drag rather than recognizing a higher source.
challenge.q: What criticism is implied by the conqueror worshiping his tools?

answers: From catching people to gathering great spoil and rejoicing in conquest
From rescuing people to building cities
challenge.explanation: The image progresses from catching to gathering, rejoicing, and continued domination.
challenge.q: How does the fisherman image develop through the passage?

answers: Whether the conqueror may continue killing nations without mercy
Whether the fisherman knows how to swim
challenge.explanation: The final question challenges the conqueror’s limitless violence and lack of compassion.
challenge.q: What moral question closes the chapter?
